items.passage: Kagiso never hurried. At the rural post office he stood at the counter with his hat in his hands while the clerk weighed a parcel of seed catalogs, and he answered every question about the rain twice. Marcus, the surveyor from Cape Town, waited behind him with a loan document that needed the farmer's signature before the afternoon bus, tapping the paper against his leg. The clerk, counting stamps, remarked that Kagiso's late wife had run this counter for thirty years. Marcus barely heard. A minute later the clerk added that the brass scale had been hers, and that Kagiso came every week to have it checked, though he rarely mailed anything. Marcus looked at the weights, worn smooth at the handles. He thought of the six-month extension his office liked to call a favor, and he slid the document back into its folder. When Kagiso finally turned around, Marcus asked him about the rain. Outside, the bus driver honked once and pulled away down the gravel road.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a visitor's impatience at an errand, then shows how details revealed in stages unsettle his aim.
It presents a farmer's slow habits at a post office, then shows how a clerk persuades him to sign a new loan.
It presents a surveyor's errand in the countryside, then shows how missing a bus forces him to stay overnight.
It presents a clerk's memories of a former coworker, then shows how those memories strain a friendship.

items.passage: Bao did not like surprises. As captain of the river freighter, he had found Wira curled among the rice sacks two days out, and now, docked below the terraced hills outside Hanoi, he had brought the boy home to eat because there was nowhere else to put him. Bao's mother set out bowls and chopsticks with the precision she gave to every meal. Wira, from an island far to the south, hesitated, then began eating with his right hand as his family always had. Bao waited for the small frown he had known since childhood. Instead his mother watched a moment, set down her chopsticks, and tore a piece of rice cake with her fingers. Bao felt the meal tilt on its hinge. Later Wira picked up the chopsticks and fumbled a dumpling into his lap, and Bao's mother laughed, a sound Bao had not heard at that table in years. Mist gathered over the terraces, erasing the lower paddies one by one.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “the meal tilt on its hinge” most nearly suggests
options: a moment of strain in which the mother's displeasure with the guest became visible.
a moment of reversal in which Bao began to regret bringing the boy into the house.
a moment of turning in which the house's familiar rules opened to another way.
a moment of imbalance in which the guest's clumsiness threatened to upset the meal.

items.passage: Dakar's Corniche was nearly empty at dusk when Yuto and Kwesi locked the shutters of their radio-repair shop for what might be the last time. Their oldest friend lay in the hospital above the promenade, and at every visit they had described customers who did not exist, a backlog of sets, a new sign. At first his face had brightened at each report. Lately he only nodded and asked about the weather. Kwesi wanted to keep the story going; it cost them nothing, he said. Yuto walked beside him along the sea wall without answering. Their kindness, he thought, had become a lantern without oil, still lifted at the bedside every evening. He remembered how their friend had begun turning toward the window whenever the shop was mentioned. At the hospital stairs Yuto stopped and said he would tell the truth tonight. Kwesi looked at the sea before nodding. Fishermen were hauling their painted pirogues up the wet sand.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a lantern without oil” most nearly suggests
options: a hope that the brothers still hold that their failing shop might soon recover.
a burden that grows heavier for the brothers each time they repeat their story.
a habit that the dying friend now depends on more than he did at first.
a gesture that continues out of loyalty though it no longer offers any comfort.

items.passage: Dario hung his uniforms on the rooftop line every morning at six, after our night shift at the bakery in Oaxaca, and I, Tendai, hung mine beside his. For months he had talked of quitting to drive a taxi with his cousin; he kept the license forms folded in his wallet and showed them to anyone who asked. That spring he showed them less often, and when he did, the creases had gone soft and gray. One morning I noticed he had begun pinning a second apron to the line, the white one the head baker gave only to those training for the ovens. He did not mention it, and neither did I. Weeks later, when I finally asked about the taxi, he shrugged and said his plans had gone out with the wash. He seemed neither sorry nor relieved, only mildly surprised, as though remembering a coat he had once owned. Below us the street vendors were unfolding their umbrellas, one stripe at a time.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “his plans had gone out with the wash” most nearly suggests that
options: his plans had been abandoned in a single decision he preferred not to discuss.
his plans had been washed away by obligations he had not anticipated at work.
his former intention had worn away gradually without any deliberate choice.
his former intention had been set aside so that it could be revisited later.

items.passage: "Careful, that bow is older than both of us," Gunnar said, grinning, as Callum fumbled it beside the cafe's sugar bowl. Trains hissed beyond the Rotterdam windows, and the conductor teased the boy about his cold coffee and his crooked collar and the way he held a fork like a bow. Callum, emboldened, asked whose bow it had been. Gunnar kept smiling, but he did not answer at once. He turned the bow slowly in his hands, thumb resting on the worn grip where another thumb had pressed first. His teacher, he said, had played with it for forty years and left it to him without a note. He mentioned this lightly, as if it were a detail about train times, and then said nothing more for a while, watching the departures board flick through cities he had no plans to visit. At last he set the bow in front of Callum and pushed it gently across the table.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From gentle teasing to mild irritation as Gunnar grows impatient with Callum's question.
From playful banter to quiet contemplation as Gunnar dwells on the bow's earlier owner.
From easy humor to open grief as Gunnar breaks down while describing his teacher.
From light conversation to formal instruction as Gunnar teaches Callum to hold the bow.

items.passage: When I was nineteen, my stepfather and I worked the dark hours at Rivka's bakery in Haifa, shaping dough before the shutters rose. He had paid my first year of tuition, and neither of us ever spoke of it; I assumed the money had simply been there. For months I treated those mornings as a sentence to be served, sulking over the cold flour and his habit of humming off-key. One morning Rivka, counting the till, said she would miss him after the holidays, when he could finally stop doing doubles. I did not ask what she meant. But I began to notice how he flexed his cracked knuckles before lifting the trays, and how he ate standing up. A week later I arrived early and had the ovens lit before he came. He looked at them, then at me, and hummed the same tune, slightly less off-key.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From sullen boredom to cheerful pride as the narrator masters the work of the bakery.
From dutiful respect to quiet guilt as the narrator learns of debts he hid from her.
From resentful reluctance to a wordless, attentive respect for the stepfather's effort.
From easy indifference to anxious concern as the narrator fears for the stepfather's health.

items.passage: When Lachlan finally carried the tin box up the lighthouse stairs in Galway, I had not spoken to him in four years, and our mother had been gone for two. The letters inside were hers, written to us during the winters she kept the light alone, and never sent. I expected complaints; she had been a sharp, impatient woman, and I had left home partly to escape her. Some letters did complain, about the damp, about our father, about me. But between the complaints she described the gannets diving at dawn, the exact color of the sea before a storm, and the biscuits she hid in a drawer for visits that rarely came. Reading them aloud, Lachlan's voice cracked on a line about my handwriting, which she had apparently kept. I did not forgive her everything. I did ask him to read that one again. Outside, the lamp began its slow turn over the water.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward her mother?
options: A lingering resentment that the letters' complaints finally confirm and justify.
A softening regard that coexists with her memory of the mother's harshness.
A complete reconciliation that erases her earlier reasons for leaving home.
A detached curiosity about letters that reveal little she did not already know.

items.passage: Gdansk in late October smells of wet grass and shipyard diesel, and that is where Milena found me, on the bench beside the field my brothers once ruled. Our house two streets away was empty except for the cracked leather ball my father had signed for each of us. I told Milena I would throw it out; keeping it felt like refusing to leave. She only said that my father had kicked the same ball to her once, badly. Then she set it down and nudged it toward the far goal. I ran after it before deciding to, and for a minute I was just a girl chasing a ball in poor light. Walking back, I noticed I had stopped holding it with both hands. At the corner a tram rattled past, its windows full of strangers going home.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To depict how a brief exchange with a friend eased the narrator's belief that keeping a keepsake is clinging
To recount an evening when the narrator and an old family friend played soccer on the field her brothers once used
To explain how the narrator and Milena decided together what should be done with the last object in the empty house
To suggest that objects left behind by parents tend to lose their meaning once the family home has been emptied

items.passage: Years later, Karim would still describe the kitchen of that Bologna trattoria as a ship's galley: narrow, brass-railed, every pot hung where the sway of a sea might have flung it. He had come only to deliver flour, and he lingered in the doorway longer than he should have. Assunta was correcting her new daughter-in-law's pasta for the third time: too thick, too dry, too hurried. Each time, her voice carried out to the long table where the family sat, and each time an uncle laughed and called the old woman a tyrant. The bride rolled the dough again. From where Karim stood, though, he could see what the table could not. Before every sharp word, Assunta tipped a little water from her own glass into the bride's bowl, and the dough, which had been cracking at the edges, began to hold. Every correction was a rope thrown, not a blow. When the plates finally went out, the uncle praised the pasta and asked which of the two women had made it. Assunta named the bride without hesitation, and Karim left the sacks by the stove.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a rope thrown, not a blow” most nearly suggests that Assunta's corrections are
options: quiet help for the bride disguised as scolding.
a harsh lesson that the bride will later come to be grateful for.
a performance staged mainly to amuse the relatives at the table.
a way of reminding the bride who truly controls the kitchen.

items.passage: We had argued for weeks about the table. I wanted the terrace laid the Galician way for my mother's visit, with octopus on wooden plates and bread torn by hand; Genevieve insisted on the long French lunch her grandmother used to serve, course after careful course. Both of us worked nights at the hospital, and we fought the way tired people fight, in clipped sentences over cold coffee at seven in the morning. I kept a list of every dish she rejected, and I was proud of how long it had grown. On the morning itself, both mothers arrived early. I found them in the kitchen, mine rolling crêpe batter far too thick and hers slicing octopus with a bread knife, each doing the other's dish badly and neither apologizing. I touched the list in my pocket. Seventeen items, I recalled, numbered in my neatest hand. We set out both kinds of plates, and Genevieve, catching my eye across the terrace, mouthed the number seventeen, which meant she had found it on the dresser days ago. Below us the vines dripped from the night's rain.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From cheerful anticipation to nervous unease about how the two mothers will get along
From cool detachment to lingering resentment over the many dishes Genevieve rejected
From tense rivalry to quiet sorrow about the weeks the two women lost to arguing
From weary irritation to sheepish humor about the narrator's own grievance

items.passage: Rain beaded on the manuscript pages Jiayi had carried to the stone bridge, and she shielded them with her sleeve while Haoran read. He had translated four of her novels and liked to say that he read her endings first, the way some people taste the sauce before the noodles. Tonight he lingered over the opening chapters, laughing aloud at a scene in a fish market and quoting a line about a stubborn aunt back to her twice. Jiayi teased him for performing, and he bowed to the lanterns as if they were an audience. When he reached the last pages, he read them quickly, squared the stack, and began to tell her about a noodle shop that had opened behind the temple. She waited for the joke about the sauce. He offered her the pages instead, holding them by the corners so the rain would not spot the final chapter, the one she had rewritten six times. Traffic hissed over the wet stones. Jiayi tucked the manuscript under her coat and asked, in an even voice, whether the shop stayed open late.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From playful banter to a subdued sense that the ending has failed
From uneasy suspicion to relief once Haoran handles the final chapter with care
From quiet sadness to renewed hope that the ending can be improved once again
From polite formality to barely concealed anger at Haoran's empty compliments

items.passage: Albuquerque in October smells of roasting chiles, and the seed-saving cooperative behind my church smells of paper envelopes and dust. I was labeling squash seed there when Nova walked in, eleven years after she had stopped coming to Mass, and asked whether we still needed volunteers. Yona, who runs the cooperative and has opinions about everyone, raised her eyebrows at me over the scale. I asked Nova nothing beyond whether she knew beans from squash. She said she had grown up sorting both. I have heard a great many confessions, and I have come to distrust the long ones; the shortest are often followed, much later, by the true account. So I let the afternoon pass in envelopes. Nova sorted the speckled bean seed from the plain faster than I could, pausing only once, over a packet labeled in her late grandmother's slanted script, which she set aside without comment. I did not ask about it. By evening the long table was covered in small brown packets, and I found that she had labeled each of hers in a hand very much like the one on the packet she had set aside.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Nova's return?
options: Wary of her motives and quietly determined to uncover why she left the church
Disapproving of her absence but too courteous to say so in front of Yona
Patient with her silence and observant of what her actions may be revealing
Overjoyed by her return and hopeful that she will soon attend Mass again

items.passage: Smell of wet stamps and coal smoke filled the little rural post office outside Tbilisi every winter morning, and Lucia, nineteen and certain she was meant for somewhere larger, breathed it like a sentence she was serving. Tatiana had run the counter for thirty years. She was slow with the register, slower with gossip, and she kept her ledgers in an order no one else could follow, which Lucia mocked to anyone who would listen. That week Lucia misrouted a parcel of medicine to the wrong village and hid the receipt inside one of those ledgers, sick with dread. Tatiana, who opened every ledger every evening, said nothing about it. On Thursday she announced that her knees needed the mountain air and took the old van out alone over the frozen pass, returning at dusk with a basket of walnuts and, folded inside her glove, a signature from the right village. I have since come to think that her famous slowness was mostly a decision about what not to notice in public. Lucia stayed four more years, and in time she, too, learned to keep the ledgers in an order no one else could follow.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Tatiana?
options: Critical of her for hiding a serious mistake from the villagers who were affected
Amused by her slow and old-fashioned habits behind the post office counter
Sympathetic to her but more interested in Lucia's restless wish to leave the valley
Appreciative of the tact with which she quietly repairs Lucia's mistake

items.passage: Bergen had given Jens a new job and a damp apartment, and when I visited, he brought me straight to the bookbinder's workshop where he now spent his days. We argued within the hour about glue. He said the animal glue was better; I said he only liked it because the old man who owned the shop liked it. Neither of us raised the week's notice he had given me before he left, or the letters I had not answered since. He pressed a spine between two boards and turned the screw, and I watched him check the binding by letting the book fall open on the bench, gently, the way a doctor lifts a wrist. Our friendship, I thought, had become a book sewn with too few stitches. Later he showed me a ledger he had rebound for a shipping firm, its pages lying flat under the lamp, and told me the old one had looked fine on the shelf for decades and split the first time anyone needed to read it straight through. I said nothing about glue after that.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a book sewn with too few stitches” most nearly suggests that the friendship
options: looks whole but may not survive an honest reckoning.
has been permanently damaged by the friends' argument over glue.
is growing sturdier as the two friends share work in the shop.
matters chiefly for the memories the friends once recorded together.

items.passage: Sit this match out, Ephraim said, and did not look up from his list. Kamal had carried the plantation's baseball nine for four summers, ever since the old owner had laid out a diamond between the tea terraces of his Ohio estate to keep the pickers' sons from idleness. The old owner had also paid for Ephraim's schooling and, before he died, asked him to look after the boy. Now a new manager had come from Cincinnati with nephews of his own to play, and it was the new manager who signed Ephraim's wages. Kamal sat on the bench beneath the drying sheds without complaint, which was worse. To the town, the choice looked like simple arithmetic: one star against a household. To Ephraim it was a rope pulled from both ends. He penciled the nephews into the order, erased one, wrote him in again until the paper thinned. In the fourth inning a nephew struck out, and the crowd's noise drifted up the hill like steam off a kettle, while Ephraim kept his eyes on the list as if it might still change.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a rope pulled from both ends” most nearly suggests that Ephraim
options: has lost control of the team to the new manager and his nephews.
is torn between two loyalties making opposing demands.
is reluctant to choose between players whose skills seem equal.
has quietly decided to defy the new manager on Kamal's behalf.

items.passage: Snow keeps no calendar. So I learned in the winter of my twentieth year, when the coach from Hamburg stalled beside a forester's cabin and two of us, strangers, were left to wait out the drifts. Grant was an Englishman with a cough and a great many opinions, and he called me Miss Ottilie with elaborate care, as though my name were fragile. He trimmed the lamp each evening with a small pocketknife and then set it on the sill, apart from his other things, never in his pocket. On the second night he admitted that it was not his; a woman on a ferry had lent it to him eleven years before, and he had never found her again. That knife, he said, had become a debt that gathered interest. He told me he had once nearly mailed it to the ferry company and had stopped at the post office door, because returning it to a stranger at a desk seemed worse than keeping it. By morning the drifts had reached the shutters, and he asked, too casually, whether I ever traveled by ferry.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a debt that gathered interest” most nearly suggests that the knife
options: weighs on Grant more heavily with each year it goes unreturned.
has grown more valuable as a keepsake from the woman on the ferry.
reminds Grant of a sum of money he still owes to the ferry company.
has become a tool Grant depends on more and more during his travels.
